units.tr: on the 8th day before the Kalends of May,
Printed in the workshop of Voegelin.
IN THE PRINTING HOUSE OF VÖGELIN

units.la: Matrum, quae in hominum deformum difpi-tatione versantur, ut ait Cicero in primo de legibus, nihil est profecto probabilius, quam plane intelligi nos ad iustitiam esse natos, neque opinione, sed natura constitutum esse [?].
units.tr: Among all the matters debated among men, as Cicero says in the first book of De legibus, nothing is surely more probable than the clear understanding that we are born for justice, and that right is established not by opinion but by nature.

units.la: Ex hoc dicto Ciceronis perspicuum est, quanta gratia debeatur Aristoteli, qui in quinto libro Ethicorum eruditas definitiones et distinctiones in-stituit et iuris tradidit, cuius partim ex coniunctione tritiora, partim ex ipsis minimis [?] habuit.
units.tr: From this saying of Cicero it is clear how great a debt of gratitude is owed to Aristotle, who in the fifth book of the Ethics set out learned definitions and distinctions and handed down the law of justice. He drew these partly from the common usage of speech and partly from the very springs of nature.

units.la: Alia ergo iustitia universalis, alia particularis. Sunt autem duae species iustitiae particularis: distributiva et commutativa, nec sunt plures.
units.tr: There is therefore one universal justice and another particular justice. There are two species of particular justice, distributive and commutative, and there are no more.

units.la: Ut autem triplex est dicendum de Deum, de quo Cicero pluribus ait: Primum est bonitas cum Deo coniuncta. Secundum ergo nos ipsos, in quo ratio est operae, ut mortui animi tantum pareant, ne aliud gerunt. Tertium [illegible, ~12 letters] iuris exultent, alios bonitates. Tres definitiones inter iustitiae tradit.
units.tr: Just as there are three kinds of duty, the first toward God, of which Cicero spoke most weightily, the second toward ourselves, in which care must be taken that the movements of the mind obey reason, and the third toward others, so three definitions of justice are handed down.

units.la: Omnium, quæ in hominum doctorum disputa-tione versantur, ut ait Cicero in primo de legibus, nihil est profecto præstabilius, quam plane intelligi nos ad iusticiam esse natos, neque opinione, sed natura constitutum esse ius.
units.tr: Of all the matters debated among learned men, as Cicero says in the first book of De legibus, nothing is surely more excellent than the clear understanding that we are born for justice, and that right is established not by opinion but by nature.

units.la: Ex hoc dicto Ciceronis perspicuum est, quanta gratia debeatur Aristoteli, qui in quinto libro Ethicorum eruditas definitiones & divisiones iusticiæ & iuris tradidit, easq; partim ex consuetudine sermonis, partim ex ipsis naturæ fontibus hausit.
units.tr: From this saying of Cicero it is clear how great a debt of gratitude is owed to Aristotle, who in the fifth book of the Ethics set out learned definitions and divisions of justice and right, and drew them partly from the common usage of speech, partly from the very springs of nature.

units.la: Alia, inquit, est iustitia universalis, alia particularis. Sunt autem duæ species iusticiæ particularis, distributiva & commutativa, nec sunt plures.
units.tr: There is, he says, one universal justice and another particular justice. There are two species of particular justice, distributive and commutative, and there are no more.

units.la: Ut autem triplex est ordo hominis, primus erga Deum, de quo Cicero grauissime dixit: Prima est homini cum Deo societas. Secundus erga nos ipsos, in quo danda est opera, ut motus animi rationi pareant, ne velut incustoditi & passim vagantes liberius exultent. Tertius erga alios homines: Ita tres definitiones iusticiæ universalis tradi solent, una à vera Dei Ecclesia, Altera à Platone, Tertia ab Aristotele.
units.tr: Just as there is a threefold order of man: the first toward God, of which Cicero spoke most gravely: "The first is the fellowship of man with God." The second toward ourselves, in which care must be taken that the movements of the mind obey reason, lest they run free like unguarded and wandering things. The third toward other men. Thus three definitions of universal justice are customarily handed down: one from the true Church of God, the second from Plato, the third from Aristotle.

units.la: Iustitia uniuersalis secundum Ecclesiæ doctrinam est integra conformitas motuum cordis, & omnium virium cum Deo seu cum lege Dei. Idem est enim dicere, congruere cum Deo, & congruere cum lege Dei, quia Deus talis est, sicut se in lege descripsit.
units.tr: Universal justice, according to the doctrine of the Church, is the complete conformity of the movements of the heart and of all the powers with God, or with the law of God. For to say to agree with God is the same as to agree with the law of God, because God is such as he has described himself in the law.

units.la: Plato iusticiam uniuersalem sic definit, ut sit obedientia omnium virium erga rectum iudicium rationis, id est, conseruatio ordinis diuinitus instituti.
units.tr: Plato defines universal justice thus: it is the obedience of all the powers to the right judgment of reason, that is, the preservation of the order instituted by God.

units.la: Eandem definit Aristoteles esse obedientiam erga omnes leges honestas ad nos pertinentes, ut Aristides nominatur iustus, quia non violat ullam legem honestæ societatis, in qua versatur.
units.tr: Aristotle defines the same as obedience to all honorable laws that pertain to us, so that Aristides is called just because he violates no law of the honorable society in which he lives.

units.la: Descriptio iusticiæ à Clemente Alexandrino tradita, Δικαιοσύνη ἐστὶ κοινωνία [illegible, ~12 letters] μετὰ ἰσότητος, Iusticia est communicatio, qua Deus se nobis communicat, & est conseruatio ordinatæ æqualitatis, complectitur uniuersalem & particularem iusticiam. Ac prior quidem pars loquitur de prima tabula, & de actionibus diuinis in renatis. Altera vero de actionibus ordinatis erga proximum.
units.tr: The description of justice handed down by Clement of Alexandria: Justice is a communion [Δικαιοσύνη ἐστὶ κοινωνία] ... with equality [μετὰ ἰσότητος]. Justice is communication, by which God communicates himself to us, and it is the preservation of ordered equality. It embraces universal and particular justice. The former part speaks of the first table and of the divine actions in the reborn; the latter of actions ordered toward the neighbor.

units.la: Etsi autem multæ sunt definitiones iustitiæ particularis apud Platonem in primo & secundo [illegible, ~8 letters] : tamen definitio Simonidis, quam Iurisconsulti amplexi sunt, admodum concinna est, dextre intellecta conuenit utriq; speciei, commutatiuæ & distributiuæ : Iustitia est constans & perpetua voluntas, suum cuiq; tribuens.
units.tr: Although there are many definitions of particular justice in Plato in the first and second [books], the definition of Simonides, which the jurists embraced, is quite elegant. Rightly understood, it fits both species, commutative and distributive: justice is a constant and perpetual will to give each person his due.

units.la: Altera diuisio iustitiæ his verbis ab Aristotele recitatur : Iustitia particularis, aut est commutatiua, aut distributiua. Commutatiua est quæ seruat æqualitatem Arithmeticam in contractibus & pœnis sine discrimine personarum. Distributiua est, quæ recte ordinat personas seruata Geometrica æqualitate.
units.tr: Aristotle recites another division of justice in these words: particular justice is either commutative or distributive. Commutative justice is that which preserves arithmetic equality in contracts and penalties, without regard to persons. Distributive justice is that which rightly orders persons while preserving geometric equality.

units.la: Huius diuisionis eruditissima ratio est: Iustitia particularis gubernat omnes actiones in societate. Quicquid autem agimus cum aliis, est aut rerum communicatio, aut personarum ordinatio. Manifestum est igitur duas esse species iustitiæ particularis, quarum altera personas ordinat, altera regit rerum communicationes, & constituit æqualitatem Arithmeticam.
units.tr: The reasoning behind this division is most learned. Particular justice governs all actions in society. Whatever we do with others is either a communication of goods or an ordering of persons. It is therefore manifest that there are two species of particular justice: one orders persons, the other regulates the exchanges of goods and establishes arithmetic equality.

units.la: Si quis autem requirit, unde sumserit Aristoteles hanc pulcerrimam collationem specierum iustitiæ ad Arithmeticam & Geometricam proportionem, nihil est quod expedire tam facile pos-simus. Nam Plato, cuius discipulus [illegible, ~7 letters] fuit Aristoteles, in sexto de legibus, cum summa venustate & gravitate disputat, æqualitatem Arithmeticam non solum in contractibus, sed etiam in omni compensatione rerum efficiendam esse, Geometricam vero, quæ & Tyrannidem & popularem licentiam prohibet, salutarem esse ciuitatibus.
units.tr: If anyone asks where Aristotle took this most beautiful comparison of the species of justice with arithmetic and geometric proportion, there is nothing we can explain so easily. For Plato, whose disciple Aristotle was, argues with great charm and gravity in the sixth book of the Laws that arithmetic equality must be effected not only in contracts but in every exchange of goods, while geometric equality, which forbids both tyranny and popular license, is salutary for states.

units.la: Arithmetica Analogia est, in qua positis tribus aut pluribus numeris, omnes distant æqualibus differentijs. Hanc recte accommodat Aristoteles ad rerum communicationem, quæ vagatur in infinitum. Non posset autem in infinitum procedere, nisi seruaretur Arithmetica æqualitas, quia vna pars generis humani exhauriretur & periret.
units.tr: Arithmetic proportion is that in which, when three or more numbers are set out, all differ by equal differences. Aristotle rightly applies this to the communication of goods, which spreads out without limit. But it could not proceed without limit unless arithmetic equality were preserved, because one part of the human race would be drained and perish.

units.la: Geometrica Analogia est, cum tribus aut pluribus terminis dispositis, non numerorum differentia consideratur, sed seruatur æqualitas proportionum. Diuiditur autem Geometrica in continuam & discretam. Continua est, quæ in tribus terminis consistit, Discreta nominatur, in qua termini quatuor, sex aut plures inter se comparantur.
units.tr: Geometric proportion is that in which, when three or more terms are set out, the difference of the numbers is not considered, but the equality of the ratios is preserved. Geometric proportion is divided into continuous and discrete. It is continuous when it consists of three terms; it is called discrete when four, six or more terms are compared with one another.

units.la: Hoc discrimen ideo recitatur, vt facilius declarari possit, quæ species Geometricæ proportionis ad iusticiam distributivam congruat. Nam in distributiva iusticia non habet locum proportio continua. Sunt enim duo termini rerum, & duo personarum constituendi, qui non pariunt continuam proportionem.
units.tr: This distinction is recited so that it can more easily be shown which species of geometric proportion fits distributive justice. For continuous proportion has no place in distributive justice. There are two terms of things and two of persons to be set up, and these do not produce a continuous proportion.

units.la: Et[?] quoniā in distributiva iusticia utendū est per mutata proportione, ex Euclide assumatur huius argumentationis descriptio. Est ergo ἐναλλὰξ[?] λό-γος, id est, permutata proportio seu ratio vicissitudinis, sumtio antecedentis comparatæ ad antecedentem, & consequentis ad consequentem, ut sicut se habent 8. ad 4. ita se habent 2.ad 1. Ergo ἐναλλάξ[?], Sicut se habent 8.ad 2. Ita 4.ad 1.
units.tr: And since in distributive justice one must use a permuted proportion, let a description of this argument be taken from Euclid. There is therefore an alternate ratio [ἐναλλὰξ λόγος], that is, a permuted proportion or ratio of interchange: the taking of antecedent compared with antecedent and consequent with consequent. For example, as 8 is to 4, so 2 is to 1; therefore alternately, as 8 is to 2, so 4 is to 1.

units.la: Nunc si placet hanc formam argumentandi ad iusticiam distributivam accommodemus. Sicut in Geometrica proportione discreta rationes inter se comparantur: Ita in distributiva fit collatio personarum & officiorum, & quæruntur personæ aptæ singulis generibus, ut sicut se habent scientia rei militaris & eloquentia, sic se habent Cæsar & Cicero. Ergo sicut Cæsari committendus est exercitus, ita Ciceroni mandanda est togata administratio. Hæc forma argumentandi vocatur argumentum ex permutata proportione.
units.tr: Now, if it pleases, let us apply this form of argument to distributive justice. Just as in discrete geometric proportion ratios are compared with one another, so in distributive justice persons and offices are compared, and persons fitted to each kind of office are sought. Thus, as skill in military affairs is to eloquence, so are Caesar and Cicero. Therefore, just as the army is to be entrusted to Caesar, so civil administration in the toga is to be committed to Cicero. This form of argument is called the argument from permuted proportion.

units.la: Cum autem noticiæ sint gubernatrices actionum, Aristoteles optimo ordine adiungit partitionibus iusticiæ sapientissimam distinctionem legum naturæ & iuris positivi, quia iustitia in hominibus est velle & imperare membris conformia legi.
units.tr: Since notions are the governors of actions, Aristotle very fittingly adds to the divisions of justice the most wise distinction between the law of nature and positive law, because justice in men is the will and command that the members conform to the law.

units.la: Ac leges quidem naturæ sunt noticiæ principiorum practicorum, & conclusionum ex his extructarum de regendis moribus, congruentes cum æterna & immota norma mentis divinæ, insitæ nobis divinitus, ut sint testimonia, quod sit Deus, & qualis sit, & regant nos, ut congruat obedientia nostra cum voluntate Dei.
units.tr: The laws of nature are notions of practical principles and of conclusions drawn from these concerning the regulation of morals, agreeing with the eternal and unchanging norm of the divine mind, implanted in us by God, so that they are witnesses that God exists and what kind of being he is, and they govern us so that our obedience may agree with the will of God.

units.la: Ius vero positivum est decretum legitimæ potestatis, non pugnans cum iure naturæ, sed addens ad ius naturæ circumstantiam aliquam probabili ratione, non necessario definitam.
units.tr: Positive law, however, is a decree of lawful authority, not contradicting the law of nature but adding to the law of nature some circumstance defined on probable grounds and not necessarily.

units.la: Sed inter ius naturæ, & ius positivum hoc interest, quod cum ius naturæ loquatur de genere, & habeat suas demonstrationes, & ubique sit idem, & neq; tolli neq; abrogari possit, ius positivum loquitur de specie, & ratum est partim propter autoritatem legislatoris, partim propter probabilem rationem, nec ubiq; idem est, deniq;[?] mutari & solet & potest.
units.tr: But between the law of nature and positive law this difference lies: the law of nature speaks of the genus, has its own demonstrations, is everywhere the same, and cannot be taken away or abrogated; positive law speaks of the species, and is valid partly on account of the authority of the lawgiver and partly on account of probable reason, is not everywhere the same, and finally is and can be changed.

units.la: Discernatur etiam summum ius ab æquitate. Etsi enim genere congruunt, quia utroq; probantur recta & damnantur contraria, tamen gradibus differunt propter circumstantias.
units.tr: The highest right must also be distinguished from equity. Although the two agree in kind, since both approve what is right and condemn what is wrong, they differ in degree because of circumstances.

units.la: Est igitur summum ius cum leges seuere sine mitigatione retinentur, etiam cum propter circumstantiam aliquam probabilis ratio erat mitigationis.
units.tr: Therefore the highest right remains when the laws are enforced strictly and without mitigation, even when some circumstance gives a reasonable ground for mitigation.

units.la: ἐπιεικεια[?] vero seu æquitas est probabilis mitigatio summi iuris in aliqua circumstantia, præsertim in casu, de quo non principaliter lex loquitur.
units.tr: Equity [ἐπιείκεια], or fairness, is a reasonable mitigation of the highest right in some circumstance, especially in a case that the law does not primarily address.

units.la: Et quoniam ἐπιεικεια[?] aut publica est, aut priuata, publicam illam quæ in iudiciis versatur Magistratibus & Iurisconsultis relinquamus, qui sapientissime disputant, utrum iudicandum sit ex scripto iure, an æquitas extra scriptum quærenda sit, priuatam vero, cuius tres sunt gradus, nisi exercebimus, nihil dilectioni erga proximum relinquemus.
units.tr: Since equity [ἐπιείκεια] is either public or private, let us leave public equity, which concerns the courts, to the magistrates and jurists, who debate with great wisdom whether a judgment must be made from the written law or whether equity must be sought beyond the written text. But unless we practise private equity, which has three degrees, we will leave no room for love of our neighbour.

units.la: Primus gradus est eleganter ferre communes hominum infirmitates, quæ non puniuntur legi[?]bus. De hoc gradu Plinius dixit: Qui vitia odit, homines odit. Nemo enim sine vitiis nascitur Optimus ille est, qui minimis urgetur, ut ait Horatius.
units.tr: The first degree is to bear with the common weaknesses of men gracefully, weaknesses that the laws do not punish. Pliny spoke of this degree: "He who hates faults hates men." For no one is born without faults. He is the best man who is troubled by the smallest, as Horace says.

units.la: Secundus gradus est, ambigua facta non calumniose in deteriorem partem flectere, non levia errata odiose amplificare, nec arcana traducere, sed tegere & sanare.
units.tr: The second degree is not to twist ambiguous deeds to the worse part in a spirit of malice, not to magnify slight errors with hatred, and not to drag hidden matters into view, but to cover them and heal them.

units.la: Tertius gradus est, ante contumaciam candide & amanter monere errantem & peccantem, & hoc officio revocare eum in viam. Hi tres gradus in vita latissime patent, & nunquam dilectioni desunt occasiones in his declarandæ lenitatis & æquitatis.
units.tr: The third degree is, before stubbornness sets in, to admonish the one who errs and sins frankly and lovingly, and by this duty to bring him back onto the right way. These three degrees extend very widely through life, and occasions to show gentleness and fairness in these ways never fail love.

units.la: Sit autem doctrina de æquitate eo nobis gratior, quia Euangelium est dulcissima [illegible, ~9 letters] legis divinæ.
units.tr: Yet the teaching about equity should be all the more welcome to us, because the Gospel is the sweetest [obscura] of the divine law.

units.la: Nam Deus non solum dispensat de ordine naturæ, sed etiam de sua lege, cuius ordo firmior est, quam ordo in caussis physicis, ut ostendit historia primorum parentum. Etsi enim hic ordo sancitus erat, ut primi parentes propter peccatum extinguerentur: tamen Deus placatus intercessione ac deprecatione filii pœnam æternam eis remisit, & pœnas in hac vita inenarrabili bonitate mitigavit. Ipsum vero Euangelium nullam admittit dispensationem, sed manet immota regula: Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam, Qui non credit in eum, jam judicatus est.
units.tr: For God dispenses not only from the order of nature but also from his own law, whose order is firmer than the order of physical causes, as the history of our first parents shows. For although this order had been decreed, that the first parents should die because of sin, God, appeased by the intercession and entreaty of the Son, remitted the eternal punishment for them, and in his inexpressible goodness softened the punishments in this life. But the Gospel itself admits no dispensation, and the rule stands unchanged: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life; he who does not believe in him has already been judged."

units.la: Postremo recitat Aristoteles gradus delictorum pugnantium cum iustitia & iure. Alia inquit, delicta sunt voluntaria, alia inuolun-taria.
units.tr: Finally, Aristotle recites the degrees of wrongdoings that conflict with justice and right. Some offences, he says, are voluntary, others involuntary.

units.la: In doctrina, quam Iurisconsulti profitentur, tres gradus delictorum traduntur, dolo facta, culpa, item casu facta. Et culpae gradus lata, leuis & leuissima.
units.tr: In the teaching that the jurists profess, three degrees of wrongdoing are handed down: deeds done by deceit, by fault, and likewise by chance. And the degrees of fault are gross, slight, and very slight.

units.la: Dolus proprie nominatur delictum, ad quod concurrunt mens sciens quid sit agendum, & voluntas libera contra rectum iudicium faciens. Hic gradus plurimum habet turpitudinis, quia maior est contumacia voluntatis, quando mens videt quid agat.
units.tr: Deceit [dolus] is properly the name for a wrong to which a mind that knows what must be done and a free will acting against right judgment both contribute. This degree has the greatest baseness, because the obstinacy of the will is greater when the mind sees what it is doing.

units.la: Culpa lata est, cum quis crassa negligentia peccat, non tamen affectata, vt cum aliquis rebus suis salvis amittit depositum, quia hoc forte negligentius custodiuit.
units.tr: Gross fault is when someone sins through crass carelessness, yet not with deliberate intent, as when someone, with his own goods safe, loses a deposit because he kept it too carelessly.

units.la: Etsi autem disputatur, An lata culpa sit dolus: tamen recte dicitur, toto genere distare dolum & culpam, id est, peccata ignorantiæ, & omissionis non affectatæ, vt infinitum discrimen est inter lapsum Euæ, & negligentiam Mariæ amittentis filium, quem putabat esse in comitatu amicorum.
units.tr: Although it is disputed whether gross fault is deceit, it is nonetheless rightly said that deceit and fault differ entirely in kind, that is, sins of ignorance and of unintended omission. There is an infinite difference between the fall of Eve and the carelessness of Mary, who lost her son, whom she thought was in the company of friends.

units.la: Reliqui sunt gradus leuis culpa & leuissima, quæ ignorantiam circumstantiarum aut negligentiam leuiorem continent, vt si quis non tribuat nomen consulis Magistratui in alio oppido, cuius ipse non est ciuis, ignorans eum esse consulem.
units.tr: There remain the degrees of slight fault and very slight fault, which involve ignorance of circumstances or a lighter negligence, as when someone does not give the title of consul to the magistrate in another town, of which he is not a citizen, not knowing that he is consul.

units.la: Hæc sunt præcipua capita, quantum ego existimare possum, de quibus disserit Aristoteles in quinto Ethicorum, qui inter omnia Philosophica scripta de virtutibus velut gemma insignis eminet. Utinam vero in scholis concionantem iustitiam placide audiamus, eiq; iuste viuendo obtemperemus, cum hæc vna sit non ἀρχὴ disciplina & vera Philosophia, vt præclare & sapienter à Platone in sexta epistola scriptum est.
units.tr: These are the principal heads, as far as I can judge, which Aristotle discusses in the fifth book of the Ethics, which stands out among all philosophical writings on the virtues like a remarkable jewel. Would that we might gladly hear justice expounded in the schools and obey it by living justly, since this alone is the [ἀρχὴ] discipline and true philosophy, as Plato wrote in his sixth letter, admirably and wisely.

units.la: An prima figura syllogismorum ideo sit perfectissima, quia aliarum duarum figurarum syllogismi ad hanc reduci possunt?
units.tr: Is the first figure of syllogisms therefore the most perfect, because the syllogisms of the other two figures can be reduced to this one?

units.la: An doctrina Galeni de contrarijs saporibus pugnet cum Aristotelis sententia, cum ille contrarios esse dicat acrem & acerbum, hic vero dulcem & amarum?
units.tr: Whether Galen's doctrine of contrary tastes conflicts with the opinion of Aristotle, since the former says that the contraries are the sharp and the bitter, while the latter says they are the sweet and the bitter?

units.la: An recte à Platone dictum sit, Philosophos esse iustos, quod in veri inuestigatione versentur, cum nihil in vitæ societatem conferre videantur?
units.tr: Whether Plato was right to say that philosophers are just because they are engaged in the search for truth, since they seem to contribute nothing to the life of society.

units.la: Hæc sunt præcipua capita, quantum ego exti-mare possim, de quibus disserit Aristoteles in quinto Ethicorum, qui inter omnia Philosophica scripta de virtutibus pulcherrima & omnium insignis est. Vtrum vero Philosophi ... [?]
units.tr: These are the principal heads, as far as I can judge, which Aristotle discusses in the fifth book of the Ethics, which is the most beautiful of all philosophical writings on the virtues and outstanding among them all. But whether philosophers ... [?]

units.la: An prima figura syllogismorum ideo sit per-fectissima, quia alias figuras ad eam reducunt, pollicet ad hanc reductio possunt.
units.tr: Whether the first figure of syllogisms is therefore the most perfect, because the other figures are reduced to it, since reductions to it are possible.

units.la: Wan eis aber eine Iunge nimyth [?]

units.tr: Of a certain field ... or sling ...

units.la: Mit sanfter yost ins prodis [illegible, ~5 letters]
Vnd d feller gesares, mit gusserm sen [?] [illegible, ~4 letters]
Si gen seter setes, est si libr conneda [?]
Alla sete sete, wie at alla sete wiede [illegible, ~4 letters]
